question_text: What do you understand by 'moral integrity' and 'professional efficiency' in the context of corporate governance in India? Illustrate with suitable examples. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Moral integrity and professional efficiency in corporate governance
topics: Moral integrity and professional efficiency in corporate governance
keyPointers: Integrity is doing the right thing when the account can be dressed up
Efficiency is doing the work well; it is not a substitute for honesty
A firm can be efficient and corrupt, or honest and slack
Governance needs both, and the board is where they are supposed to meet

points.text: In a company, moral integrity is the refusal to cheat the shareholder, the worker or the public. Professional efficiency is the ability to run the business well.
A bank that hides a bad loan is efficient at the concealment and empty of integrity. A public firm that is honest and never delivers a project has integrity without efficiency.
Satyam showed integrity failing at the top. A well-run company that also tells its bad news shows the two together.
Corporate governance is the arrangement that stops efficiency from being used as an excuse for the lie.

question_text: 'International aid' is an accepted form of helping 'resource-challenged' nations. Comment on 'ethics in contemporary international aid'. Support your answer with suitable examples. (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: Aid can be help, or it can be a lever
The ethical test is who decides, and whether the receiving people are the purpose
Tied aid, a political condition and a vanished fund are the failures
Good aid builds a capacity and then becomes unnecessary

points.text: Aid is ethical when it meets a need the recipient named, and unethical when it buys a policy or a contract.
Tied aid that must be spent on the donor's firms, or a grant that demands a strategic concession, uses the poor as an instrument.
A famine relief that arrives, is accounted for, and leaves a local system stronger passes the test. A prestige project that the country did not ask for does not.
The ethics of aid is dignity and a purpose that survives the donor's interest.

question_text: “Corruption is the manifestation of the failure of core values in the society.” In your opinion what measures can be adopted to uplift the core values in the society? (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Corruption as a failure of core values
topics: Corruption as a failure of core values
keyPointers: A bribe is easier where honesty is no longer admired
Values are lifted by example, by a school and by a cost for the cheat
A sermon without a consequence teaches the opposite lesson
The family, the office and the public figure all teach

points.text: Corruption spreads where people stop believing that honesty is what their own group rewards.
Schools that practise fairness, a family that does not boast of a shortcut, and a leader who is punished when caught, lift the value more than a pledge.
A simple rule, a transparent service and a whistle-blower who is not destroyed make the honest act cheaper than the corrupt one.
Core values rise when the society the child can see actually lives them.

question_text: In the context of work environment, differentiate between 'coercion' and 'undue influence' with suitable examples. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Coercion and undue influence at work
topics: Coercion and undue influence at work
keyPointers: Coercion is a threat. Undue influence is a pressure that uses a relationship
One frightens the will. The other captures it
Both produce a yes that is not a free yes
The remedy is a way to refuse without losing the job or the bond

points.text: Coercion forces a choice by a threat. Undue influence steers a choice by abusing trust, authority or dependence.

A manager who threatens dismissal unless a false figure is signed is using coercion. A senior whom a junior reveres, and who quietly asks for a personal favour the junior cannot judge, is using undue influence.
The first is open and frightening. The second looks like loyalty, which is why it is harder to see and to resist.
A fair workplace treats both as a stolen consent, and gives the junior a route that does not depend on the same person.

question_text: “The simplest acts of kindness are by far more powerful than a thousand heads bowing in prayer.” – Mahatma Gandhi. What does this quotation convey to you in the present context? (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: Gandhi ranks a done kindness above a performed piety
The present temptation is to post the prayer and skip the act
A small concrete help is the test of the feeling
The line is against display, not against prayer itself

points.text: Gandhi is saying that a religion or a public morality which does not change how one treats a person nearby has failed.
In the present, a forwarded prayer, a vigil or a corporate pledge is easy. Sitting with a patient, paying a worker on time, or stopping a cruelty in one's own office is the harder and smaller act.
He does not ban prayer. He says a prayer that never becomes a kindness is the weaker thing.
The quotation asks for conduct that a neighbour could notice, not for a devotion that only the devotee can see.

question_text: “To awaken the people, it is the women who must be awakened. Once she is on the move, the family moves, the village moves, the nation moves.” – Jawaharlal Nehru. What does this quotation convey to you in the present context? (Answer in 150 words)
subTopics: Women as the start of a social change
keyPointers: Nehru treats the woman as the first mover, not as a beneficiary who comes last
A household changes when the person who runs it can decide
The present gap is still education, safety and a paid recognition of her work
Awakening is her agency, not a scheme about her

points.text: Nehru's line puts the education and freedom of women at the start of any national waking, not at the end.
A woman who can study, earn and refuse a harmful custom changes the child, the spending of the house and the politics of the village.
The present context is a rising enrolment beside a remaining violence, an unpaid care load and a thin presence in work and in the assembly.
The nation moves when she moves as a person with a choice, not when she is moved by a programme.

question_text: “Do not hate anybody, because that hatred which comes out from you must, in the long run, come back to you. If you love, that love will come back to you, completing the circle.” – Swami Vivekananda. What does this quotation convey to you in the present context? (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: Hate is not spent when it is expressed; it trains the hater
A public hatred comes back as a harder politics and a frightened self
Love in the quotation is a practice, not a mood
The circle is social as well as personal

points.text: Vivekananda is warning that hatred reshapes the person who sends it, and then returns from the world he has made.
A rumour, a boycott or a daily contempt looks like an attack on someone else. It also narrows the attacker and invites the same weapon back.
In the present, a social-media hatred scales the circle: it comes back as polarisation, a retaliatory lie and a society that cannot do ordinary work together.
The alternative he offers is not softness. It is the decision to complete a different circle.

question_text: “What really matters for success, character, happiness and lifelong achievements is a definite set of emotional skills – your EQ – not just purely cognitive abilities that are measured by conventional IQ tests.” Do you agree with this view? Give reasons in support of your answer. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: EQ, IQ and what success actually needs
topics: EQ, IQ and what success actually needs
keyPointers: IQ opens a door. EQ decides what the person does in the room
The view is right to demote IQ and wrong if it discards it
Character and a lasting achievement need both
Emotional skill can be practised; it is not a consolation prize

points.text: The view is largely right, with one correction: emotional skill matters more than the line admits only because cognitive skill is already assumed.
A high IQ without self-control, empathy or the ability to hear a criticism produces a brilliant person who cannot hold a team, a friend or a purpose.
Happiness and character are plainly closer to emotional skill than to a test score. A difficult achievement still needs the cognitive ability to understand the problem.
Agree that EQ is neglected and decisive. Do not agree that IQ is a dispensable extra.

question_text: Differentiate ‘moral intuition’ from ‘moral reasoning’ with suitable examples. (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: Intuition is the immediate sense that something is wrong
Reasoning is the account of why, which can correct the sense
One is fast and fallible. The other is slow and also fallible
A good decision lets the intuition raise the alarm and the reason check it

points.text: Moral intuition is a quick judgment felt before an argument. Moral reasoning is the argument that tests it.
A person who flinches at a bribe before he can say why is using intuition. The same person, listing the duty, the harm and the alternative, is reasoning.
Intuition can be a prejudice that feels like a conscience. Reasoning can be a clever excuse. Each needs the other.
They differ in speed and in the demand for a reason. Neither is safe alone.

question_text: Is conscience a more reliable guide when compared to laws, rules and regulations in the context of ethical decision-making? Discuss. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Conscience against law as a guide
topics: Conscience against law as a guide
keyPointers: Conscience sees the case. The law sees the class of cases
A private conscience can be braver than a bad rule, and also more biased
Reliability comes from using both, not from crowning one
The hardest decision is a lawful act that conscience still refuses

points.text: Conscience is sometimes the better guide, and it is not reliably the better guide.
A law can be unjust, slow or silent, and a conscience that refuses it has, at times, been right. A conscience can also be anger, loyalty or a self-serving story.
Rules exist because private judgment disagrees, and a public standard is needed. Conscience exists because a rule cannot name every case.
The reliable guide is a conscience that can say why, checked against a law that can be criticised. Neither replaces the other.

question_text: ‘Probity is essential for an effective system of government and socio-economic development.’ Discuss. (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: Probity is honesty that can be checked, not a private virtue
A government without it spends trust before it spends money
Development leaks where the contract, the exam and the licence are for sale
Effectiveness and probity are not rivals

points.text: Probity is the habit of using public power only for the purpose it was given, in a way others can verify.
Without it, a scheme reaches the contractor rather than the beneficiary, and a citizen stops believing the next scheme.
Investment, a tax and a social trust all assume that the rule is not secretly for sale. Development slows where that assumption dies.
Probity is not an ornament on an effective state. It is one of the conditions of effectiveness.

question_text: What were the major teachings of Guru Nanak? Explain their relevance in the contemporary world. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Teachings of Guru Nanak and their present relevance
topics: Teachings of Guru Nanak and their present relevance
keyPointers: One God, an honest work and a sharing of what is earned
He rejected caste, empty ritual and the separation of the householder from the holy
The teaching is a social ethic, not only a theology
It is relevant wherever identity is used to rank people

points.text: Guru Nanak taught a direct devotion, an honest living and a duty to share, and he refused the rank of caste and the show of ritual.
Naam, kirat and vand chakna — remember the one God, earn by honest work, and share — summarise the practice. He also rejected the idea that a holy life required leaving the world.
The contemporary use is against a communal ranking, a corrupt livelihood, and a religiosity that performs and does not feed.
The teaching remains relevant because the failures it named are still ordinary.

question_text: Explain the term social capital. How does it enhance good governance? (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: Social capital is trust and a network that lets people act together
It lowers the cost of a rule because people expect others to follow it
A neighbourhood that trusts can watch a service and a school
The capital can also exclude, if the network is a closed one

points.text: Social capital is the trust, the norms and the associations that let strangers cooperate without a contract for every act.
Good governance is easier where a citizen believes the official and the neighbour will keep a rule. Complaints are made, taxes are nearer to being paid, and a local body is watched.
A self-help group, a resident association or a traditional council can supply that trust. A network that serves only its own caste can also block a fair governance.
Social capital enhances governance when the trust is wide. A narrow trust enhances only the group that holds it.

question_text: You are an executive in a nationalised bank. A close colleague, a widow from a lower-middle-class family, says her father needs heart surgery costing about ₹10 lakh and she has no insurance. You can only offer sympathy. Weeks later she says the surgery succeeded because the bank manager quietly released ₹10 lakh from someone else's dormant account, on the promise that it stay confidential and be repaid. She has begun repaying. (a) What are the ethical issues involved? (b) Evaluate the behaviour of the bank manager from an ethical point of view. (c) How would you react to the situation? (Answer in 250 words)
topic: A dormant account used for a colleague's surgery
topics: A dormant account used for a colleague's surgery
subTopics: Public money and a private mercy
keyPointers: The need is real and the method is a breach of trust
A manager may not spend a depositor's money because the cause is kind
Secrecy makes the mercy unauditable
The right reaction helps the colleague without joining the concealment

points.text: Ethical issues: a genuine medical need, misuse of a depositor's dormant money, a breach of fiduciary duty, a demand of secrecy, and your own duty once you know.

The manager's kindness does not rescue the act. He had no authority to lend a third person's balance. Repayment reduces the loss; it does not erase the breach, the risk to the depositor, or the precedent.
Compassion would have been a bank scheme, a staff welfare fund, a transparent advance, or a collection. A secret draw on a dormant account is the opposite of those.

You should not stay silent. Tell her the arrangement must be regularised, urge the manager to disclose it to the proper authority, and if he will not, report it yourself, while helping her find a lawful way to finish the repayment.

question_text: On 20 July 2023 a midnight landslide, about 60 km from Uttarkashi, killed and trapped many people. You are the District Magistrate and have reached with doctors, NGOs, media and police. A man asks for help for his pregnant wife, who is in labour and losing blood. Doctors say she needs an immediate transfusion. The ambulance has blood-collection bags and test kits, and some team members will donate. You know, as an AIIMS-trained physician, that blood for transfusion should come only from a recognised blood bank. The team is split. Doctors will conduct the delivery if they will not be penalised for transfusing. (a) What are the ethical issues involved? (b) Evaluate the options available to you as District Magistrate. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: An emergency transfusion with no blood bank
topics: An emergency transfusion with no blood bank
keyPointers: The rule exists to prevent a mismatched or infected transfusion
The place and the hour make the recognised bank unreachable
A life in front of you changes the weight of a safety rule
The decision should be recorded, not hidden, and the doctors protected if they act in good faith

points.text: Ethical issues: the duty to save a named life, the safety rule that blood should come from a bank, the risk of a mismatch or an infection, a divided team, and your duty not to ask doctors to break a rule and then punish them.

Options: wait for banked blood and likely lose the patient; allow a tested voluntary donation and an immediate transfusion, with consent and a written order; or evacuate, which the bleed may not allow.
Waiting honours the rule and abandons the woman. A secret transfusion protects no one. Evacuation is right only if it is actually faster than the bleed.

The responsible option is a group-tested voluntary transfusion, documented on the spot, with the doctors assured they acted under your written direction in a disaster, and a report to the health authority as soon as the night allows.

question_text: Rashika, a Joint Secretary, is still in office at 9 pm on Saturday. Her husband travels for an MNC; their children, aged 5 and 3, are with a domestic helper. At 9.30 her superior asks for a detailed note for a Monday meeting, which means working on Sunday. She had wanted this posting and has put people's welfare first, but she has repeatedly left a sick child with a nanny and feels she has failed her family. She now wants a line beyond which personal life comes before punctuality, hard work and selfless service. (a) Discuss the ethical issues. (b) Briefly describe at least four laws for a healthy, safe and equitable working environment for women. (c) If you were in her place, what would you suggest to mitigate such conditions? (Answer in 250 words)
topic: A Joint Secretary asked to give up Sunday
topics: A Joint Secretary asked to give up Sunday
subTopics: Work, care and a reasonable limit
keyPointers: Dedication is a virtue until it consumes the person who has a dependent
A superior's urgency is not automatically an ethical claim on a Sunday
The burden falls harder on the mother because the care is assumed to be hers
The remedy is a boundary said in advance, and a workplace that does not punish it

points.text: Ethical issues: duty to public work, duty to two small children, a gendered load of care, a superior's power to extend the day, and the difference between a real emergency and a habit of late calls.

Four laws: the Maternity Benefit Act, the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, the Factories Act and related labour provisions on hours and safety, and the Code on Wages together with equal-remuneration rules. The child-care duties under the Maternity Benefit Act, including a crèche in larger establishments, belong in the same list.

In her place, separate a genuine midnight crisis from a note that can be scoped tonight and finished by a team on Monday morning. Say the limit once, in writing, and propose a roster so the same officer is not the default.

Suggest a crèche, predictable hours, and a culture in which a father's travel is not treated as the mother's unlimited shift. Selfless service that deletes a family is not a sustainable ethic of the service.

question_text: Vinod, an honest IAS officer, has just become Managing Director of the State Road Transport Corporation, his sixth transfer in three years. The Chairman, a powerful politician close to the Chief Minister, is accused of irregularities. An Opposition board member gives Vinod documents and a video of the Chairman demanding a bribe for a large order of QMR tyres, and recalls that the Chairman cleared that firm's pending bills. The member will not expose the Chairman himself, and hints that if Vinod does, public support and, later, the Opposition's patronage will follow. Vinod may be punished and transferred if he acts. He also sees that the member wants to use him. (a) Evaluate Vinod's options as a conscientious civil servant. (b) Comment on the ethical issues arising from the politicisation of bureaucracy. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: A bribe video and a political invitation
topics: A bribe video and a political invitation
keyPointers: The video is a lead, not a brief for either party
Exposing a bribe is a duty; doing it as someone's campaign is not
A sixth transfer is pressure, and it is not a reason to look away
The file should go to a process that neither the Chairman nor the Opposition owns

points.text: Options: ignore the material; leak it for the Opposition; confront the Chairman privately; or authenticate what he can and send it to the vigilance agency and the Chief Secretary, without becoming the member's candidate.

Ignoring protects his posting and abandons the public. A private warning invites a cover-up. A political leak makes him a partisan and taints the proof. The conscientious route is a formal, documented report to the lawful authority, with the video kept intact.
Politicisation creates exactly this trap: frequent transfers to soften an officer, and an opposition that offers protection in exchange for a useful scandal.
The ethical issue is a service that is punished for honesty and rented by whoever expects to win. Vinod's answer is to serve the process, not the next government.

question_text: You are the new Additional Director General of the Central Public Works Department. Your Chief Architect, retiring in six months, is staking his reputation on a major project. Seema, a newly joined Senior Architect trained at Manchester, suggests changes that would improve the project and shorten it. The Chief Architect turns insecure, humiliates her in front of colleagues and raises his voice. She is losing confidence and is thinking of resigning. You need her contribution and you need the project finished. (a) What are the ethical issues? (b) What options do you have to complete the project and retain Seema? (c) How would you respond to her predicament, and what would you institute so this does not recur? (Answer in 250 words)
topic: A retiring architect and a humiliated colleague
topics: A retiring architect and a humiliated colleague
keyPointers: Credit is not a property of the senior person
Humiliation is an abuse of rank, not a style of review
The project needs her idea and his experience, in that order of fairness
A private word is not enough; the conduct has to stop in public

points.text: Ethical issues: a senior using rank to protect his legacy, a loss of dignity, a risk to her mental well-being, a gendered pattern of correction-in-public, and the organisation's interest in the better design.
Options: do nothing until he retires; move her off the project; or keep both, put the design discussion in a minuted meeting, and stop the public humiliation at once.

You should meet her, record that her suggestions will be examined on merit, tell him privately that the behaviour ends, and if it continues, start the formal conduct process. Credit for an adopted idea is named.

Institute a written channel for a technical dissent, a harassment redress that a junior can use without meeting the same senior, and a review in which the retiring officer is honoured for delivery rather than for being the only author.

question_text: Your 11-year-old son is found wandering during class. He has become a loner, stopped answering, and failed a football trial. He finally says classmates call him stunted, duh and a frog in class and on the students' WhatsApp group, and he names them but asks you to let it rest. At a later match, a colleague's son shows you a caricature video and points out the boys. You walk past and go home. Next day a viral video accuses you, your wife and your son of physically bullying those children on the field. A junior suggests a counter-video. You post your own video from the event, identify the likely perpetrators, narrate what happened, and speak about the misuse of social media. (a) Discuss the ethical issues in the use of social media. (b) Discuss the pros and cons of your using social media to counter the fake propaganda. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: A child's bullying and a viral counter-video
topics: A child's bullying and a viral counter-video
subTopics: Social media, a child and a public reply
keyPointers: A platform scales a cruelty and then a reply, with no time to cool
Naming children in public is a harm of the same family as the original mockery
Silence lets a lie settle. A video can spread the child's humiliation further
The proportionate route is the school and the platform's report tool, not a second viral

points.text: Ethical issues: bullying of a child, a lie about a parent, the permanence of a post, the temptation to answer in the same currency, and the duty not to expose other minors.

Pros of the counter-video: it puts a fact against a viral lie, shows there was no assault, and warns others about misuse. Cons: it identifies children, escalates a feud, can make your own son more visible, and uses a public office-holder's reach in a private fight.
A better use of the medium is a short factual denial without names, a report to the platform, and the evidence given to the school and, if needed, to the police.
Social media is ethical when it corrects a lie with the least exposure. It is unethical when a wounded parent turns other children into content.
